verdict.root_cause: cartservice is not running: its process dies during startup while initializing the Redis cart store, because the Redis endpoint it is configured with (redis-cart on the non-default port 6380) refuses the connection, and the exception is unhandled at the entrypoint so the container never reaches a listening state [tr_92f99225aba3]. Automation wrote exactly that value — REDIS_ADDR set to redis-cart:6380, previously unset — at 12:19:29, two minutes before the checkout alert, as part of a recurring override/revert cycle [tr_fbc86148aeb9]. With nothing bound on cart's port, frontend's checkout path gets TCP-refused dials at :7070 and reports gRPC 14 UNAVAILABLE plus a code 13 INTERNAL naming the cart dependency [tr_dad74a47ac9a], and checkoutservice's PlaceOrder requests start but never reach a completion stage [tr_c5b5317af34a]. The wrong address value is itself the failure mechanism.
verdict.reasoning: Cart's own logs show a repeating connect-fail-crash cycle rooted in Redis store initialization from main, with no successful listen line, so cart is absent rather than slow [tr_92f99225aba3]. Frontend sees a refused connection with empty metadata at the client receive-status stage, which is what a caller observes when nothing is bound; DNS, auth/TLS, and downstream slowness were ruled out on error shape [tr_dad74a47ac9a]. Checkoutservice logs PlaceOrder starts with no completion and no error lines, consistent with a synchronous call into an unavailable dependency [tr_c5b5317af34a]. The port recorded in cart's failing dials matches the REDIS_ADDR value written at 12:19:29 [tr_fbc86148aeb9], making the config value the mechanism, not just an upstream act. Frontend's partial degradation (peaks ~34%, min 0) fits a dependency only some paths touch [tr_5c2a944a87e6].
open_questions: Frontend error crossings begin at 11:23:30 and cart-refused errors already appear at ~11:22 [tr_5c2a944a87e6][tr_dad74a47ac9a], an hour before the 12:19 REDIS_ADDR override and inside a change-free cart gap from 08:55 to 11:41 [tr_fbc86148aeb9] — an earlier, distinct cause of cart unavailability may have preceded this one.
Whether redis-cart actually listens on 6380 or only 6379 was never verified directly; no redis-cart dispatch was run.
cartservice liveness/restart and resource series returned nothing usable [tr_333036e98333], so crash-loop is inferred from logs alone and OOM/external kill is not absolutely excluded.

alternatives.root_cause: The redis-cart backend itself is down or not serving, so cartservice cannot initialize regardless of the address it was given.
alternatives.why_not: Cart's failures are refused connections on a non-default port that was written into config minutes before the alert [tr_92f99225aba3][tr_fbc86148aeb9]; no evidence was gathered on redis-cart, and the port mismatch explains the refusal without requiring Redis to be unhealthy.

alternatives.root_cause: An earlier cartservice image change (hotfix tag applied at 11:41) left the service unable to start, and the 12:19 REDIS_ADDR edit is coincidental.
alternatives.why_not: The crash stack points specifically at the cache connect step rather than a general startup defect [tr_92f99225aba3], and the dialed port matches the configured override rather than the image change [tr_fbc86148aeb9].

retrieved:
/ Confirming it: The change record shows the variable and both values. A configuration pointing at an address
that no longer answers usually produces connection errors in the service's own logs with the
address quoted verbatim - the fastest confirmation available, because the wrong value appears

/ Confirming it: Change history is the first and usually the only query needed: an image reference that changed
inside the incident window, on the service the alert names or one hop upstream of it. Logs
confirm the shape of the failure; they rarely identify it faster than the change record.

/ Before proposing it: A prior configuration for this service must exist in change history, and the incident's
evidence must name a configuration or flag change inside its window.

proposal.expected_effect: Restoring cartservice's pre-12:19:29 environment (REDIS_ADDR back to unset/default) and recreating the container should end the startup crash loop: in Loki {service="cart-service"} the repeating redis-cart:6380 connect failure plus unhandled Redis-cart-store-init exception lines cease and normal AddItemAsync/GetCartAsync lines resume as at 10:22; in {service="frontend"} the code 14 UNAVAILABLE dials to :7070 and the code 13 INTERNAL naming cart stop; frontend error ratio falls from ~0.075 back toward the ~0.020 baseline with no new crossings; checkout-service PlaceOrder starts are again followed by payment/email/queue-write lines.
proposal.if_wrong: Falsified if cart-service still logs connect-failure-plus-startup-exception after the recreate, meaning redis-cart really listens only on 6380 (never verified directly, no redis-cart dispatch run) or redis-cart is itself down. Falsified as a full explanation if cart recovers but frontend crossings continue, since errors began ~11:22-11:23 inside the 08:55-11:41 cart change-free gap, an hour before this override. Also not durable if the ~4-5h automation cycle re-applies the override with no operator action.
proposal.risk: If the intended endpoint really is 6380, this revert keeps cart crash-looping and burns the recovery window. The recreate is unconditional and discards cart's in-process state; if the true exit is an external kill (OOM only inferred from logs, liveness/resource series unusable) the container dies again for an untouched reason. Reverting also races the live automation harness's next write.
proposal.blast_radius: cartservice is recreated. Callers frontend (cart/checkout paths), checkoutservice PlaceOrder and loadgenerator traffic already see total cart failure, so added harm is small. redis-cart sees cart traffic move off 6380 to the default endpoint; paymentservice, emailservice and accountingservice see order volume resume.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Critical alerts on frontend and checkoutservice within seconds of each other span the user-facing checkout path, which is not dismissible and no open incident covers it. The shared timing across two independent seeds suggests a common downstream dependency, but nothing in the alerts pins a class yet.
